content: JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN PERSONALITY 16, 179-192 (1982) T ssessment of Motivation within MICHAEL HAYMES RiverView Hospital for Children AND LOGAN GREEN Durham Hill Reports progress in the development of a research tool for the assessment of the three developmentally earliest, within Maslow’s framework, conative needs (physiological, safety, belongingness). Scores on the Needsort were derived ac- cording to Kagan’s conceptualization of motive description. item analyses, item selection methods, reliability studies, and validation studies across a broad range of populations are discussed. These studies employed both factor-analytic and comparative (analysis of variance) methods. Safety-need scores discriminated among persons varying in social and cognitive development. Preliminary analyses of belongingness needs among disturbed children supported Eron’s recent con- clusions concerning the possible ways to prevent development of overly ag- gressive behavior among populations with high risk for such behavior disorders, Conative research has until relatively recently focused aimost exclu- sively on the characterization of “self-actualized” individuals (who are in a minority in the cultures in which these studies are undertaken). Compared to self-actualization studies, there have been relatively few investigations of developmentally earlier needs. The potency of Maslow’s approach as an interpretive tool for understanding the variation among the majority of people (i.e., those less than self-actualized) has been subjected to comparatively little investigation (cf. Aronoff, 1967; De- poyster, 1971; Green & Haymes, 1977; Haymes & Green, 1977; Lollar, 1974; McClelland, 1978; Nelli, 1980; Simpson, 1976; Wilson, 1976; Wilson & Wilson, 1977). This paper discusses the development of an inventory (the Needsort) of early motives which is based on Maslow’s (1943a, The order of authors’ names was determined by random procedure and is not indicative of disproportionate contributions to the overall research. 180 HAYMES AND GREEN 1970) motivational theory and Kagan’s (1972) conceptualization of the structure and description of motivation. The Needsort was developed to aid the study of earlier needs both because these are the natural concerns of developmentally younger in- dividuals and because these earlier needs are frequently implicated in references to growth arrest or delay in conative development. Studies using the earlier needs as important constructs have been hampered by the lack of a conceptually clear measuring device which is easy to ad- minister, score, and interpret. A motive (cf. Kagan, 1972; Maslow, 1943a, b, c) is a cognitive representation of a desired goal that the person thinks will make him or her feel better. The role of uncertainty and its resolution in defining goals has been treated as an underlying energizing element in both Maslow’s (1937, 1943a) and Kagan’s (1972) frameworks. The individual is continually creating representations of experience. Uncer- tainty is the felt incompatibility between cognitive representations and experience or behavior. Popular motives typically ascribed to people in Western culture, such as achievement, affiliation, power, dependency, and nurturance, can be conceptualized as derivatives of a primary motive to resolve uncertainty and alleviate subsequent affective distress. cause each person’s threshold for discomfort is a relatively individual function, the degree of distress is best described in relative rather than absolute terms (Kagan, 1972). Therefore, the terms that have been uti- lized to describe the qualitative component of motives (e.g., strength, intensity, or amplitude) need to be embedded in a more comprehensive consideration of the individual’s spectrum of needs. Kagan (1972) has developed a terminology that is more appropriate to describing a mental representation’s relative motivational quality than do the “strength” terms ordinarily used. The “articulation” of a motive refers to the degree of specification of the central dimensions of that goal. One measure of articulation of a motive is its distinctiveness in terms of some other motive. The “com- plexity” of a motive refers to the elaboration and breadth of the concept. An appropriate measure of complexity (to be discussed later) is its prom- inence in the mental imagery of the individual, where prominence may be defined “by the number of exemplars recognized as belonging to the (motive)” (Kagan, 1972, p. 61). The “ascendency” of a motive “ap- proximates the popular term preoccupation” (Kagan, 1972, p. 61). An appropriate index of a motive’s ascendency is its retrievability, i.e., its availability to consciousness, such that information processing is selec- tive in its favor. Finally, the clarity of a motive may be defined as the extent to which the cognitive representation of that goal state stands out from among the other conative goals and thereby orients the person to relate his or her experience to the goal and to seek out experiences that are likely to gratify it. Clarity is a function of both prominence and

ASSESSMENT OF MASLOW’S NEED CATEGORIES 181 retrievability of motives. The Needsort makes use of these descriptive terms, particularly clarity, rather than the usual notions of intensity and amplitude, in describing relative need prepotency. Maslow has addressed the same issues (with somewhat less conceptual refinement) by emphasizing the hierarchical nature of needs and their stagewise (as opposed to stepwise) emergence. Conative development, as discussed by Maslow (1943a), involved an unidimensional definition of personosocial maturity running through a stagelike progression of increasingly integrated and differentiated cognitive representations of separable (in terms of their social survival functions) primary goals. These goals were described, in developmental order, as the needs for physiological competency, personal, physical, and psychological safety, belongingness, esteem, and cognitive understanding (Maslow, 1970).’ A conative goal becomes prepotent (i.e., exerts a dominant influence over one’s perceptual interpretation of his or her social world) quite a few years after the initial entry of that particular motive into one’s life as an important guiding force, and after the individual has attained the necessary resources for meeting the demands of earlier goals. The need for esteem, for example, would not become the major conative director of a person’s social schemas until such time as that person felt that he or she had the interpersonal resources for (a) staying safe (i.e., whole) in the social world and for (b) successfully role playing (Turner, 19.55) to be capable of fulfilling one’s desires for belongingness and affiliation (Erikson, 1973; Haymes & Green, 1977). The conative domains to be represented were derived from Maslow’s various descriptions (e.g., 1937, 1970) of the physiological, safety, and belongingness needs. The problem of socially desirable response bias is particularly difficult to combat when the respondent is asked to choose whether he or she prefers a socially approved goal to ones that are relatively less acceptable. In our society (cf. Emling, 1977; Lundberg, 1974), behaviors that are performed in the service of a developing sense of self-worth are more likely to be regarded positively than are those behaviors motivated by, and in the service of, feelings regarding the reduction of fear and of loneliness (i.e., safety and belongingness needs). Because there is good reason to believe that need ’ Kagan also described a set of secondary motives which derive from specific environ- mental presses local to each society. These include (in Western countries) the needs for achievement, power, and dependency. They are seen as serving to resolve the uncertainty (and thereby alleviate subsequent affective distress) stemming from any of the primary concerns. This distinction between primary (fairly universally human) and secondary mo- tives is quite useful. Although Maslow emphasized this distinction. too, it was sometimes blurred in his own writings. For example, he wrote of the role of the secondary motives for power and achievement in the gratiJicarion of the esteem needs, yet he often confounded his measure of behavioral concomitants, such as dominance, superiority, and pride, with the need in whose service those behaviors and secondary motives were operating (cf. Maslow, 1937, 1970).

182 KAYMES AND GREEN for esteem items might “pull” high scores among adults when counter- posed with items representing more primitive goals, such items were not included in the Needsort. ITEM SELECTION The content for the safety and belongingness domains on the Nee was determined by inspection and categorization of the responses of 987 male and female respondents (age range, 13-73) to Aronoff’s Sentence Completion Test @CT; Aronoff, 1971; Wilson & Aronoff, 1973). The completion to each SCT stem was scored according to whichever motive (if any) it represented. The SCT is not scored for physiological needs. Therefore, physiological content was derived entirely from Maslow’s descriptions without the benefit of actual responses. Once the content was determined, prior instruments were examined for items. The majority of nonoriginal items in the final version of the Needsort were suggested by items written by DePoyster (1971), Lollar (1973, 1974), and Maslow (1945). Most of the original items were re- worked completions to the SCT. Physiological needs are tapped by items such as “It is (very-not at all) important to me to not have aching feet and legs” or “to stay warm in cold weather.” Safety concerns are represented in items such as “It is (very-not at ail) important to me to be where everybody obeys the rules and regulations” and “. . . to know who my enemies are.” Belongingness items refer to statements such as “It is (very-not at all) important for me to have friends I can really talk to” and “. . . to feel that most people who know me also like me.” The preliminary set of 90 items (30 each of physiological, safety, and belongingness) was distributed to three professionals (clinical develop- mental psychologists) and 12 graduate students (representing psychoiogy, educational psychology, curriculum theory, and sociology). These per- sons were asked to decide (on a 4-point Likert scale) the extent to which each item represented each of the needs. Items were kept that had extremely high scores on the need for which they were written and extremely low scores on the other needs. If 80% (i.e., 12 of the 15) of the judges gave the item either a 3 or a 4 on the scale for which it was meant, and 80% of the judges (not necessarily the same 80%) gave it a I or a 2 on the other two scales, the item was considered as having received an “extremely high score.” This led to the exclusion of nine items. Five other items were eliminated on theoretical grounds, and one item was dropped in order to bring the total number to 75 (i.e., 25 sets of three items each). Each set of three included a physiological, a safety, and a belongingness item. Thus, the Needsort contains 25 sets of three items each. The items within each set are representative of developmentally different motives

ASSESSMENT OF MASLOW’S NEED CATEGORIES 183 or needs. Responses indicating the personal relevance of each item are made on a Likert scale of 0 through 5. However, the respondent is not permitted to give the same score to any two items within a set of three. This serves as a built-in corrective for extreme response bias (Bentler, Jackson, & Messick, 1971) and also provides an index of prominence. The latter is determined by the number of times that an item, repre- sentative of a particular need, is ranked in either first or second place in each of the 25 sets of items. Thus, the more exemplars referring to a particular need that are chosen over those relating to other needs, the more information provided regarding the prominence of that need. (First- place items are weighed twice as much in this calculation.) This variable assesses the need’s relative ability to direct behavior. The prominence score is thus an indicator of the anxiety in one’s daily interactions gen- erated by uncertainty regarding one’s personal competencies for its sat- isfaction (Maslow, 1943a, 1970). The retrievability of a need (i.e., its availability to consciousness) is indexed by the Likert sum over all items representing that need. (Low retrievability implies lack of conscious awareness, not necessarily total lack of influence; cf. Kagan, 1972.) Kagan (1972) has suggested that motives be discussed in terms of what may be called their qualitative clarity rather than the usual physical strength metrics. The Needsort operationalizes clarity of safety needs by examining the ratio of the prominence of safety to the relative re- trievability of the lower (physiological) and higher (belongingness) needs.2 Thus, the clarity of one’s safety needs is greater (i.e., exerts more in- fluence) to the extent that both physiological and belongingness needs are relatively irretrievable and the prominence of safety needs is high. Two people may rank their safety needs equally, but the one whose average retrievability of belongingness and physiological needs is greater will not be driven by safety concerns as exclusively as will the other person. Item Analysis and Reliability Studies All item analyses are based on the Likert scores to items and their sums (retrievabilities) unless otherwise noted. For a group of 387 college sophomores and juniors, the standardized item alphas were .88, .82, and .87 for the physiological (P), safety (S), and belongingness (B) items, respectively. The average item means and standard deviations were (P) 2.89, 1.16; (S) 3.20, 1.18; and (B) 4.21, 0.94. Split-half coefficients were (P) .85, (S) .78. and (B) .82. Correlations between items and total scales on the whole sample were transformed to Fisher z’s and means calculated for each scale. The average item-to-scale correlations were (P) .71, (S) .6O, and (B) .66. Thus, the psychometric data suggest adequate reliability. Validation Studies Responses to Aronoff’s (1971) SCT served as stimuli from which to generate items for the three scales of the Needsort. How well does the content of those items really sample the kinds of things about which physiological-, safety-, and belongingness-oriented persons are expected to be concerned? The results of a series of factor analyses pointed to reasonable concurrence between the expected and depicted domains. The two samples consisted of 467 undergraduates, mean age 20, and 117 graduate students, mean age 32, with the range 21-63 for the graduate samples. Both varimax and oblimin rotations were performed on each group, with squared multiple correlations as initial communality esti- mates. All these analyses revealed a similar organization of items. There- fore, the factor analyses reported below are based on the combined sample of 584 persons and oblique rotation. Each of the scales was factored separately because interest resided in the domains that are subsumed under each of the need sets studied here. (Investigative interest was not focused on determining whether the 7.5 items would cluster into the three sets of needs, although they did to a significant degree. This latter question speaks to the validity of Maslow’s theory, a question not entertained in the current study.) It was expected that the factors to emerge would resemble Maslow’s (1970) categorization of safety and belongingness needs. His categori- zations of physiological needs have always been vague, which is to be expected, given the wide range of possibilities. All factors with an ei- genvalue of 1 or greater were rotated obliquely. Items were included if the item weight was at least .40.3 Most of Maslow’s categories were identifiable in the factors. The four physiological need factors were named (1) General Comfort, (2) Bodily Integrity, (3) Fitness and Health, and (4) Energy and Stamina. The five safety need factors were called (1) Stability and Predictability, (2) Protection from Freedom and Fear, (3) Social Structure and Order, (4) Freedom from Interpersonal Chaos, and (5) Freedom from Social Chaos. The six belongingness need factors to emerge were identified as (1) Acceptance by Wider Group, (2) Family Acceptance and Intimacy, (3) Extrafamilial Contact and Intimacy, (4) Warm and Friendly Relations, (5) Workplace Acceptance, and (6) Af- fectionate Relations with Special People. 3 These data and a copy of the instrument are available from the authors.

ASSESSMENT OF MASLOW’S NEED CATEGORIES 185 The factor-analytic results suggest that the domains of safety and be- longingness needs were indeed tapped. These results further implied that the cognitive representation of a safe world for undergraduates and grad- uate students between the ages of 20 and 63 revolves primarily around the issues of stability, protection, and freedom from fear. Less urgent (but important) for these persons were the issues emanating from the needs for structure, law, limits, and order. The cognitive representation of belongingness, and the associated anxiety, is concerned primarily with “functioning well” as part of some larger group and within the family. As an index of criterion validity, Aronoff’s XT was administered to teachers (N = 31), undergraduates (N = .54), and both psychiatric (N = 29) and elementary school (N = 40) children. Since the correlations were in the same direction and of similar magnitude, these four groups were combined to furnish an overall correlation matrix. Safety need clarity was associated positively (Y = .36, p < .05) with SCT Safety percent, negatively with SCT Belongingness percent (- .30, p < .Ol), and was unrelated to the SCT Esteem percent (- .03). Belongingness clarity followed a similar pattern, with the exception of a significant association with SCT Esteem percent (- .28, p < #OS). The correlations were r = - .23 (p < .05) with SCT Safety percent and r = .46 6j < .Ol) with SCT Belongingness percent. The person who is driven primarily by safety needs, relative to higher (developmentally more mature) needs, ought also to be functioning at more primitive levels in those areas of life which are tied intimately either to conative growth or specifically to the satisfaction of safety needs. (“Satisfaction” means that the individual has developed the re- sources necessary to meet the demands of a set of needs.) In Table 1 are summarized the results from a number of comparative studies which examined persons with low, moderate, and high safety need clarities. In addition to the analysis of variance results, gammas (a measure of ordinal correlation) are presented as an index of proportional reduction ia error. Finally, one might note that the greater the belongingness-safety dis- tinctiveness in any person’s motive structure, the greater the likelihood of that person being more conatively mature than would some other person whose belongingness and safety needs were more equivalent. The gammas between belongingness-safety distinctiveness and the test vari- ables are displayed in the last column of Table 1. For comparative pur- poses, the means for the three need clarities are displayed in Table 2. The results reported in Table 1 suggest that the construct validity of the Needsort is adequate for research purposes and that its clinical use can be investigated. On the other hand, the low correlations between safety clarity and social desirability, activity level, and impulsive temperamentality provide fur- ther evidence of validity insofar as these demonstrate that the Needsort is independent of such potentially confounding influences. Generally, the more secure individuals have achieved a greater depth of moral under- standing, get higher grades, can express their emotionality, enjoy social proximity, are nondogmatic, and reject traditional middle class and es- sentialist educational values. Furthermore, those persons whose safety needs were no longer problematic tended to deemphasize a “loser” philosophy. Although individuals whose safety needs have become less problematic tend to be capable of higher cognitive functions, the strength of relationships between safety need resolution and these other important variables (above) was unchanged when controls for intellectual potential and cognitive development were added. DISCUSSION Safety clarity scores on the Needsort successfully discriminated be- tween persons varying in their social and cognitive development. The test-retest and internal reliabilities of the three scales were within gen- erally accepted ranges, as were the correlations attesting to the criterion validity of the scales. The factor-analytic results provided evidence that the content of the items was as Maslow intended. Those individuals with Needsort scores indicating that they had resolved (met) most of their important safety-need-based concerns had characteristics which were concordant with the secure personality as described by Maslow (1943~1,

ASSESSMENT OF MASLOW’S NEED CATEGORIES 189 1970) and more recently by others investigating within Maslow’s theo- retical framework (Aronoff, 1967; Aronoff & Meese, 1971; Ashmus, Bedrosian, & Wiseman, 19.52; Green & Haymes, 1977; Haymes & Green, 1977; McClelland, 1978; Simpson, 1971; Wilson & Wilson, 1977). For example, important behavioral and attitudinal differences have consis- tently been found between individuals and groups with prepotent safety concerns and those with prepotent esteem concerns. These differences have encompassed the degree of consistency in moral action across situations (Haymes & Green, 1977; Ward & Wilson, 1980; Wilson, 1976); the level of moral development attained (Green & Haymes, 1977); cross- national psychogenic death rates (Rudin, 1968); job attitudes, perfor- mance, and leadership abilities (Steers & Braunstein, 1976); and gender role differentiation and leadership (Messe, Aronoff, & Wilson, 1972). Suggestive evidence for differences among individuals and groups at differing rungs on the earliest steps of the conative development hierarchy were provided by Lollar (1974) and DePoyster (1971) (although the mea- sures employed were subject to the social desirability biases discussed above). Thus, the Needsort makes it possible to begin to tease out the influences of earlier needs in various aspects of development; that is, to be capable of assessing the three earliest needs and their relative behavioral and attitudinal effects. We have chosen to concentrate on the clarity of safety needs for the reasons described above. However, other investigators may find it more useful to examine the belongingness clarity, or the difference between belongingness retrievability and safety retrievability (i.e., distinctive- ness). For example, on the one hand, belongingness needs and safety needs are differentially related to socioeconomic position (as indexed by parental education) among adults (Table 1). Individuals whose parents had less formal education had more lingering safety needs, yet social class was unrelated to belongingness. On the other hand, general hostility among emotionally disturbed children, although significantly correlated with both sets of needs, was much more related to underdeveloped needs for affiliation than it was to one’s needs for social safety (cf. Table 1, line 23). This supports Eron’s (1980) call for a direct inculcation of healthy dependency needs and behaviors in potentially aggressive pop- ulations. Though we concentrated on safety clarity, others’ areas of concern may more directly implicate clarity of other early needs. Im- portance of the three earliest needs embedded within the context of each other (i.e., clarity) has a lot of intuitive appeal as potentially important in making decisions for type and styles of therapeutic interventions. Safety clarity may indicate needs (initially) for more structured pro- gramming. As pointed out by Combs (1976), DePoyster (1971), and Simp- son (1976), an understanding of one’s needs would also appear to be a valuable step in individualizing instruction and planning curricula. In

190 AAYMES AND GREEN planning interventions in the more directive therapies, therapists may also find it useful to understand the clients’ needs structure in schools and other institutional contexts. Belongingness clarity vs safety clarity may be important in choosing individuals to participate in group treat- ments, especially those involving group rewards and punishments. The style of group intervention (more-or-less leader oriented) may be pre- scribed eventually using parameters which include lingering safety con- cerns and level of belongingness prepotence. It is important to recognize that the Needsort has been used by a handful of researchers and clinicians, most of whom have been in contact with each other. Furthermore, the relatively small number of studies which speak to the reliability and to the validity of the Needsort suggests the exercise of cautious optimism in generalizing the results reported above. Publication of these data at this point was undertaken because it is important that other investigators (academic researchers and chni- cians) have available to them a modestly reliable and potentially valid assessment device with which these basic needs could be meaningfuify measured.
